321: Endnotes continue. Note 7 (Ford DETERMINATION): Henry Ford (1863-1947), the son of Irish immigrants, was a school dropout. At age 15 he was a machinist's apprentice in Detroit and later worked as chief engineer of the Edison Company in Detroit until 1899, when he and others founded the Detroit Auto Company. In 1903 he founded the Ford Motor Company. He introduced the Model T in 1908, assembly-line production in 1913, the Model A in 1927, and the V-8 engine in 1932. He ran for a U.S. Senate seat and lost and at one time considered a Presidential bid. Note 8: Napoleon Hill had an abiding interest in higher education throughout his adult life. His constant theme was that education should not simply focus on 'imparting knowledge,' but on teaching students how to organize knowledge and apply it to accomplish specific objectives. After high school, he completed business school in Tazewell, Virginia, and studied law at Georgetown University Law School but dropped out due to financial reasons. In 1913 he began working in the advertising and sales department of LaSalle Extension University in Chicago. In 1916 he established the George Washington Institute to teach a correspondence course in salesmanship. In 1923 he made arrangements to purchase and operate the Metropolitan Business College in Cleveland. In 1931 he established the International Publishing Corporation of America and the related International Success University, launching Success Magazine. In 1941 he became a resident lecturer in psychology at Presbyterian College in Clinton, South Carolina. He received an honorary doctorate from Pacific International University in the late 1940s.
322: Endnotes continue. In 1962 Hill and his wife Annie Lou established the Napoleon Hill Foundation, a charitable organization steeped in educational mission, headquartered in Wise, Virginia. The associated Napoleon Hill World Learning Center is located at Purdue University Calumet in Hammond, Indiana. Through the years the Foundation has been associated with several institutions of higher learning. The editor shares a 'footnote to a footnote' connecting higher education, the Napoleon Hill Foundation, and broadcasting: Bill Lee Atchley was born in 1932 in Cape Girardeau, Missouri. Employing many success principles of The Think and Grow Rich Philosophy from an early age, Atchley overcame meager circumstances, played professional baseball in the New York Giants organization, got a doctorate in engineering, and became president of Clemson University (during which time he served on the Hill Foundation). He later was named president of the University of the Pacific and then Southeast Missouri State University. As it turns out, Atchley's wife Pat was the former Pat Limbaugh, also of Cape Girardeau. Her cousin was Rush Limbaugh III, who presided over what many consider the most successful and profitable program in the history of radio broadcasting. Limbaugh, credited with virtually reinventing the national radio talk show beginning in 1988, is one of the best examples of how using a 'Definite Chief Aim' can lead to extraordinary success.

Note 1: The Chicago Fire raged from October 8-10, 1871, destroying four square miles, including the business district. Two hundred and fifty lost their lives, 90,000 were left homeless, and property damage was estimated at $200 million. Hill must surely have had in mind a personal catastrophe also involving fire in Chicago: In 1923, after losing control of Napoleon Hill's Magazine, he returned to Chicago to get his belongings, only to find the building had been destroyed by fire. Gone were autographed photographs, important letters including some from Presidents, and, worst of all, questionnaires filled out by hundreds of eminent and successful individuals who had agreed to participate in Hill's research. Ever the positive thinker, Hill carried on, and 14 years later Think and Grow Rich was published.

325: Endnotes continue. The editor explains that Hill uses the term 'ether' rather than 'electromagnetic spectrum,' reflecting popular scientific concepts of the day. In the late 19th and early 20th century, many scientists believed an invisible substance called 'ether' permeated the universe. The Michelson-Morley experiments and Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity forced abandonment of the ether concept. The few changes in terminology made in this revised edition—such as using 'electromagnetic spectrum' instead of 'ether'—are made simply to remove stylistic impediments for today's reader. The sum and substance of Hill's ideas remain unchanged. Note 6: The quotation 'The oak sleeps in the acorn' is from As a Man Thinketh by James Allen (1864-1912), a British-born American essayist. Allen taught that the key to personal power lies within the mind. The opening sentence of his classic is 'As a man thinketh in his heart so is he'—we are what we think, and our character is the sum of all our thoughts. Hill uses variations of that tenet repeatedly in Think and Grow Rich!
326: Endnotes continue. Note 7: The 'dreamer' President was Franklin D. Roosevelt. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) was established in 1933 under the Roosevelt Administration to control floods, improve navigation, raise living standards on nearby farms, and generate electric power on the Tennessee River and its tributaries. TVA included nine major dams, 51 dams in all, interconnecting navigation locks, port facilities, 12 coal-fired generating plants, and later two nuclear plants. Combined generating capacity was more than 30 million kilowatts. Early in the New Deal, Hill served as an unpaid public relations adviser to Roosevelt, according to Hill's official biographer. He developed plans to shape public opinion, offered ideas for Roosevelt's fireside chats, and there is some suggestion he may have been responsible for the president's famous phrase 'the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.' Senator Jennings Randolph was responsible for Roosevelt's asking Hill to visit the White House. Note 8: O. Henry was the pen name of William Sydney Porter (1862-1910), master of irony and the surprise ending. He had embezzled money from the bank where he worked but received a light prison sentence, serving only three years and three months. (Work with the incarcerated was originally one of the goals of the Napoleon Hill Foundation, sponsoring courses in prisons to teach inmates the principles for success. Studies have shown recidivism is significantly reduced among prisoners who complete the studies.)
327: Endnotes continue. Note 9: 'Infinite Intelligence' is the term Hill uses to describe 'God,' or 'Divine Power,' or the 'Supreme Being' at work in the universe. His conception of God is richly textured and multi-faceted—more than a divinely spiritual, personal, moral force. God is a source of intelligence, direct communication, and exchange of information. Hill writes primarily from a Judeo-Christian perspective, but his view of Infinite Intelligence is nonsectarian and widely encompassing. Notice how Hill sees Infinite Intelligence at work in the lives of Jesus, Gandhi, and Mohammed. Hill is never 'preachy' about Infinite Intelligence, but to fully understand and utilize The Think and Grow Rich Philosophy, it is necessary to understand the part that Infinite Intelligence—God—plays in it. Note 10: 'Tramp' here means 'itinerant,' 'roving,' or 'traveling.' Note 11: Two days after Dickens' twelfth birthday, his father was jailed in a London debtor's prison. His mother sent Dickens (1812-1870) to work in a blacking factory, laboring 12-hour days in a dirty, rat-ridden warehouse, earning only six to seven shillings per week. The 'tragedy' Dickens suffered involved a failed love relationship with Maria Beadwell, daughter of an English banker. In 1830, when Dickens was 18, he fell madly in love with Maria, who was 19. Her parents considered Dickens unworthy and eventually packed Maria off to finishing school in Paris. Dickens loved her for four years, but his passion was unrequited.

Maria Beadwell is believed to have been the inspiration for the character of Dora in David Copperfield.
